_meta.description: Scripture Alone ships the American Standard Version as a signed, encrypted package — the same format a licensed translation would use. The format, the implementation, the measurements, and an honest account of what it cannot do.
_title: How a Licensed Translation Stays Safe in an Open-Source Bible — Scripture Alone
a-closed-source-bible.c65136: A closed-source Bible app is in the identical position. Any app that reads a licensed translation offline must put a key on the reader's device. That is true of every major Bible app on the App Store. The difference is not whether a key is on the device — it is whether anyone outside can confirm what the app does with it.
a-fork-gets-the.e413bc: A fork gets the code, not the text. The repository contains no content key and no signing key, and the packaging tool refuses to run against a key inside the working tree. Anyone may clone Scripture Alone; nobody who does can decrypt a licensed package, because the secret was never in the thing they cloned.
a-licensed-translation-ships.dfa869: A licensed translation ships as a signed, encrypted package. The app can read it. A person holding the file cannot read it without the key. And the publisher decides — in data the app enforces, not in a PDF in a drawer — what may be done with the text once it is open.
a-packaged-translation-is.8d2b01: A packaged translation is fully searchable — phrases included — with no plaintext index at any point. Postings carry word positions, so a phrase is an adjacency check rather than a scan, and they are bucketed by a keyed hash and sealed like chapters. A hashed-token index left in the clear would, for a Bible, let someone align frequencies against a public edition until every hash was identified. That is precisely what we did not build.

every-permission-there-is.32d0ce: Every permission there is true because that package is the American Standard Version, which is public domain — sealing it must not cost its readers anything. A licensed package is where those fields earn their keep.

four-files-carry-the.4f3b8d: Four files carry the whole claim: TranslationPackage.swift — where the part worth reading is the sequence of checks performed when a package is opened, and the two private functions that open a sealed box — together with PackagePolicy.swift, PackageSearchIndex.swift and TranslationRights.swift, plus the packaging tool. The format is implemented twice, in two languages, so a divergence shows up as a failing test rather than as a package that won't open on your desk.

so-the-american-standard.ee8e39: So the American Standard Version now ships as the package — no plaintext database in the app to fall back on, and it is the translation Scripture Alone opens by default. Every reader, on every launch, derives the content key, unwraps it from the Secure Enclave, verifies an Ed25519 signature and reads chapters decrypted one at a time. Searching it searches the sealed index. If any of that broke, the app would not open on a fresh install.
stated-precisely-so-it.cb9102: Stated precisely, so it can be checked
still-open-so-nobody.8a788e: Still open, so nobody discovers it later: the attested key-delivery route (a small endpoint that releases a key only to a genuine build, which we will build if your terms need it) is specified but not written; there is no watermarking, which we can add and would describe to you as a deterrent rather than a protection; and no package has yet had to hold two publishers' keys at once, though the design is namespaced for it.
that-is-a-stronger.9c0808: That is a stronger claim than a demonstration can make, and it is the reason to prefer it. A sample nobody selects proves the code compiles. A default translation proves the format survives contact with real use — real size, every chapter, every search, on every device, for as long as the app is in the store.
the-analogue-hole-is.bbe4b4: The analogue hole is always open
the-content-key-is.47e572: The content key is derived with HKDF from a seed injected at build time, then sealed to a Secure Enclave key generated on that device and marked this-device-only. The keychain holds ciphertext. That closes every route that actually happens — a copied keychain, a device backup, a file-system dump — and it does not hide the seed from someone disassembling the binary. Nothing on a general-purpose computer does.
the-full-paper-includes.055049: The full paper includes the complete format specification, the leakage analysis in detail, both key-delivery options, and the table of every test that asserts these properties by name.
the-header-hash-in.93de93: The header hash in the sealed data no longer matches; the seal fails.
the-header-is-plaintext.5be923: The header is plaintext on purpose. Anyone may see what a package claims to be, who signed it and under what terms, without holding any key. the-index-is-sealed.aef9bf: The index is sealed exactly like the text. A search opens one or two of 256 encrypted buckets and decrypts only the chapters its hits are in. There is no plaintext index.
the-instinct-that-public.adf1fe: The instinct that public source makes text less safe is understandable, and it is the opposite of how cryptography is assessed. Kerckhoffs's principle, the foundation of the field since 1883, holds that a system must stay secure when everything about it except the key is public. Every cipher a publisher already relies on — the TLS in front of their storefront, the disk encryption on their staff's laptops, Apple's Secure Enclave — is public in exactly this sense.
the-key-is-on.713b39: The key is on the device, and a determined attacker can recover it
the-key-isn-t.548435: The key isn't pinned; refused before its terms are read.
the-obvious-way-to.d0eac9: The obvious way to prove a format is to ship a sample beside the real translations. We did that first, and it proves only that a code path compiles.
the-package-id-in.67ef86: The package id in the sealed data no longer matches; the seal fails.

the-packaging-tool-runs.f3aa89: The packaging tool runs on the publisher's machine with the publisher's keys. We never receive the plaintext and never hold the key that decrypts it.
the-permission-policy-sits.30ca4d: The permission policy sits in a header signed by the publisher's own key. Edit the policy and the signature fails; the package stops opening.
the-plaintext-never-exists.3409e4: The plaintext never exists as a file
the-security-of-this.02c1f3: The security of this design rests on the key and the signature. That is the correct place for it to rest.
the-shipped-package-permits.8fad40: The shipped package permits everything, because its text is public domain and its readers must lose nothing. That a package can forbid things — and that the app obeys, at the control the reader touches — is proved separately, against packages built to forbid them. Proving both with one artefact would let a weakness in either hide behind the other.

what-remains-visible-to.cb83a4: What remains visible to someone without the key is the size of 256 buckets. Recovering word frequencies from that is a 256-way subset-sum over tens of thousands of unknowns, and its answer would be "bucket 37 probably holds the", which decrypts nothing. Padding every bucket to the largest would cost 6.5× the index size; we measured that rather than guessing, and the padding quantum is a signed header parameter a publisher can change.

which-buckets-a-query.f58c18: Which buckets a query opens is visible to something observing file access on a device it controls. That is inherent to any encrypted index not read in full, and reading it in full would mean decrypting the whole index per keystroke. It reveals that two searches were for the same word, not what the word was.
